title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
hook: a child's landscape often starts with one line across the page. the hymn's fifth verse stretches a line too, and then asks about it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's fourth verse: desire, the first seed of mind, and poets searching their hearts for the bond of what is in what is not. Did you catch a want underneath a plan? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

Hand a child a blank sheet and a crayon and ask for a landscape. Sometimes the first mark is a line straight across the page. That's the ground. And with that one stroke, the page has an up and a down. Sky goes above the line. Grass and roots go below. Before the line, the paper was just white. After it, there are places to put things. The Nasadiya Sukta's fifth verse draws a line too. But it's an ancient hymn, not a child's drawing, and as soon as the line is down, the verse starts asking questions about it. Today: the cord stretched across.
screen: `A BLANK SHEET, A CRAYON.` → `ONE LINE ACROSS: THE GROUND.` → `NOW THERE'S AN UP AND A DOWN.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the verse says: their cord was stretched across. Was there something below it? Was there something above it? Then it goes on: there were seed-placers, there were great powers. Their own power below, a giving forth above. The word for cord is rashmi. It can mean a ray of light, a rein, a line. Stretched across, it does what the child's crayon does. It makes a below and an above. This verse is hard, and honesty about that is part of reading it. The hymn doesn't say whose cord it is. Some readers take their to mean the poets of the verse before, the ones who searched their hearts, as if their insight drew the line between what is and what is not. Others read it differently, and the hymn leaves the question standing. Notice something else. Even while it describes, the verse keeps asking. Was there below? Was there above? A plainer hymn might simply say: and there was earth below and heaven above. This one puts a question mark on each side of its own line. Then the second half: there were seed-placers, there were great powers. And a pair: their own power below, something that holds and carries. A giving forth above, something that moves outward. One reading hears in it two halves of a whole, a receiving and a giving, needing each other. On an ordinary day, that picture can be small and close. A floor that holds a body. A breath that goes out from it.
screen: `RASHMI: A CORD, A RAY, A REIN.` · `WAS THERE BELOW? WAS THERE ABOVE?` · `WHOSE CORD? THE HYMN DOESN'T SAY.` · `HOLDING BELOW, GIVING FORTH ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the line across your own body. Sit, and feel where you meet the chair or the floor. That's your line. Below it, let yourself be held. Feel the weight going down, the ground carrying it, nothing for you to do. Above it, notice the breath, moving out and in, the part of you that gives forth. Stay with both at once: held below, breathing above. When you drift, come back to the line where they meet. If you pray, you can rest there in prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its fifth verse, a cord stretched across, a below and an above, and a question asked about each. Today's word.

Your line: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation, who really knows? Today, when you draw a line, a deadline, a boundary, a rule, ask one honest question about each side of it. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: The fifth verse of the Nasadiya Sukta is read in more than one way by Hindu commentators and modern readers, and the hymn as a whole is kept in Vedic recitation learned from a teacher.

fork.setup: you're the poet. a cord is stretched across the beginning. what do you say about the two sides?
options: earth below, heaven above, as everyone knows
was there below? was there above?
nothing: the line needs no sides
fork.reveal: the verse asks: was there something below? was there something above? it puts a question on each side of its own line.

original.note: Sanskrit: a ray, a rein, a cord. In Rig Veda 10.129.5 it is the line stretched across.

trapdoor: what you thought: a creation hymn tells you what's up and what's down.
what it means: this verse stretches a cord across, then asks whether anything was below it or above it.
what a scholar hears: tirashcino vitato rashmir esham, 'their cord was stretched across,' a line commentators read in more than one way, since 'their' is never named.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.129.5 (their cord was stretched across; was there below, was there above? there were seed-placers, there were great powers; their own power below, a giving forth above)

notes: Verse 5 is obscure. Paraphrase of 5c–d (retodhā āsan mahimāna āsan svadhā avastāt prayatiḥ parastāt) as 'seed-placers, great powers; their own power below, a giving forth above' should be checked; svadhā and prayati are hard to render.
Sanskrit of 5a (tiraścīno vitato raśmir eṣām) given from memory in simplified transliteration (tirashcino vitato rashmir esham); confirm.
'Some readers take their to mean the poets of the verse before' is offered as one reading among others; confirm it is a reading actually held, or cut to 'the hymn doesn't say'.
'One reading hears in it two halves of a whole, a receiving and a giving' is a soft interpretive gloss; confirm or cut.
Rashmi glossed as ray / rein / cord; confirm.
Editor: the teach no longer places the seed-placers below and the great powers above, which the verse does not say; varied a stock 'the hymn doesn't settle it' line used across nearby days.
